paragraphs: Active learning selects which examples should receive labels, aiming to reduce annotation needs. This paper first questions how that benefit is measured. When evaluation uses supervised learning alone, adding labeled examples changes both the available inputs and their labels. The resulting improvement therefore mixes two sources of benefit, making label efficiency harder to isolate.

The authors propose evaluating acquisition steps through semi-supervised learning, which already uses the unlabeled pool. They then introduce neural pre-conditioning, or NPC, an acquisition algorithm inspired by Neural Tangent Kernel analysis. NPC considers uncertainty about unlabeled examples while penalizing redundant choices within a candidate batch, encouraging informative labels that cover different examples.

The theoretical result concerns networks in the large-width regime: NPC improves downstream training in a way previously associated with generalization. That association is not itself a generalization guarantee. Empirically, combining NPC with a leading semi-supervised learner achieves high performance with very few labels, supporting the value of studying acquisition and unlabeled-data learning together.
neurips-2022-a-neural-pre-conditioning-a.tldr: NPC selects uncertain, nonredundant examples for labeling and evaluates label efficiency within semi-supervised learning.

paragraphs: An anomaly detector can face different data after deployment than it encountered during training. AnoShift makes this problem measurable for unsupervised anomaly detection using Kyoto-2006+, a network traffic dataset spanning ten years. Changes in user behavior and software provide naturally occurring shifts, giving the benchmark a temporal basis for evaluating generalization.

The authors examine those changes through individual features, t-SNE visualizations, and Optimal Transport measurements of distribution differences between years. They then define a testing protocol with IID, NEAR, and FAR splits. These divisions let researchers assess performance under different degrees of separation from the training distribution within one organized benchmark.

Tests involving both classical and deep learning models show performance deteriorating over time. The authors also demonstrate that addressing distribution shift can improve results relative to training that assumes independently drawn data from one unchanged distribution, reporting average improvements of up to 3% for their approach. The benchmark therefore exposes a practical weakness while providing a setting for measuring attempts to address it.
neurips-2022-anoshift-a-distribution-shi.tldr: AnoShift benchmarks how unsupervised anomaly detectors handle naturally changing network traffic over time.

paragraphs: Combining two individually manageable families of functions can create a much more complex family. This paper studies that problem using uniform covering numbers, a measure of how many representative functions are needed to approximate a class. Even when each component has a small covering number, passing one component's output into another can produce prohibitively large or unbounded capacity.

The proposed remedy is to add a small amount of Gaussian noise between the components. The authors show that this can control the capacity of the combined class, offering a way to reason about systems assembled from separate modules. Their proofs introduce covering numbers for random functions measured using total variation and Wasserstein distances.

The authors apply the theory to multilayer sigmoid networks. Preliminary MNIST results indicate that noise with an elementwise standard deviation as small as 10^-240 can improve on existing uniform bounds. This finding concerns the mathematical bounds: the stated empirical result does not claim that such tiny noise improves predictive accuracy. Its significance is that capacity control may require numerically negligible perturbations.
neurips-2022-benefits-of-additive-noise-.tldr: Adding Gaussian noise between function classes can control the complexity that otherwise grows sharply when they are composed.

paragraphs: Vision-language tasks require understanding at different scales. Answering a question about an image may depend on its overall meaning, while locating an object described by a phrase requires precise regional information. FIBER is designed to support both kinds of tasks within one architecture, addressing the separation between approaches focused on high-level understanding and those focused on image regions.

The model inserts cross-attention into the image and text backbones themselves. This lets the two streams interact deep inside their processing, instead of reserving fusion for dedicated layers after separate processing. Training also proceeds at two scales: first with image-text pairs, then with image-text examples that include box annotations.

The authors evaluate tasks including question answering, captioning, retrieval, phrase grounding, referring expression comprehension, and object detection. They report consistent improvements over strong baselines across the tested tasks, often surpassing methods trained with orders of magnitude more data. These results support the combined use of deep multimodal interaction and coarse-to-fine training for broad vision-language capability.
neurips-2022-coarse-to-fine-vision-langu.tldr: FIBER combines fusion inside image and text backbones with coarse-to-fine training to support both global and regional vision-language tasks.

paragraphs: ConfounderGAN addresses the unauthorized use of personal images for training classifiers. Its aim is to alter images so that people can still use them normally, while models trained on the altered dataset struggle to learn the intended relationship between images and labels. The intervention operates on the training data by adding carefully generated noise.

The generator creates image-specific noise with a confounder property: it introduces misleading correlations between images and labels. Those correlations interfere with learning the correct mapping. A discriminator constrains the noise to remain small and visually imperceptible, connecting the learning-disruption objective with preservation of the images' normal utility for human viewers.

Experiments cover six classification datasets, split between natural objects and medical images. The authors report better results than existing leading methods in standard settings and applicability to fast encryption scenarios. Transferability and stability experiments provide further evidence for the approach. The stated protection is therefore demonstrated through its effect on image learning, with the reported evaluations supporting the usefulness of confounding noise.
neurips-2022-confoundergan-protecting-im.tldr: ConfounderGAN generates visually subtle noise that creates misleading image-label correlations to obstruct unauthorized classifier training.

paragraphs: D^2NeRF learns to separate moving objects from a stationary environment using a video from a single camera. It builds a three-dimensional scene representation through self-supervision, extending the separation problem beyond individual images. The intended decomposition includes moving shadows, which also change the observed scene even though they are not separate solid objects.

The method uses two neural radiance fields, one for the static background and one that can change over time. Simply combining those fields creates a problem: the more flexible dynamic field can absorb content that belongs in the static field. A new loss encourages the intended separation, while an additional shadow field network identifies and separates moving shadows.

The authors introduce a dataset containing varied moving objects and shadows. They demonstrate that the method can outperform leading approaches in separating dynamic and static 3D content, removing occlusions and shadows, and segmenting moving objects in images. The contribution connects these tasks through one scene decomposition, with explicit mechanisms for controlling the dynamic representation's flexibility.
neurips-2022-d-2nerf-self-supervised-dec.tldr: D^2NeRF separates moving objects and shadows from a static 3D environment learned from a single-camera video.

paragraphs: Risk-averse reinforcement learning emphasizes unfavorable returns, but that focus can cause learning algorithms to overlook successful strategies. The authors prove that, under certain conditions, this produces a barrier at a local optimum. Their concern is therefore both what an agent should optimize and whether its learning procedure can discover strategies that improve that objective.

They introduce soft risk to bypass this barrier and pair it with a cross-entropy sampling module. The sampler preserves risk aversion despite the softened optimization and also improves sample efficiency independently. Separating these responsibilities allows training to sample episodes with poor conditions while still learning from strategies that succeed within them.

The combined algorithm, CeSoR, can be added to any risk-averse policy gradient method. Experiments in maze navigation, autonomous driving, and resource allocation show improved risk aversion, including scenarios where standard risk-averse policy gradients fail completely. These findings support separating difficult-condition sampling from the optimizer's treatment of returns, rather than relying on one mechanism to perform both jobs.
neurips-2022-efficient-risk-averse-reinf.tldr: CeSoR separates risk-focused sampling from softened optimization to improve risk-averse policy learning and bypass a conditional local-optimum barrier.

paragraphs: Multivariate time series contain several measurements evolving together, often from a common source such as one patient. Their usefulness depends partly on relationships between channels, including how those relationships change over time. COSCI-GAN targets these shared dynamics, which typical generative models can struggle to capture even when individual channels contain plausible patterns.

The framework coordinates generation in two ways. Individual time series begin from a common point in latent space, reflecting their shared origin. A central discriminator then encourages the generated channels to preserve their joint dynamics. These mechanisms make relationships among features an explicit concern of the generation process, alongside producing the separate series.

Experiments with medical and financial data show that the approach helps preserve channel correlations and produces synthetic data that performs well in downstream tasks. This matters because classifiers and predictors can use information carried by interactions among measurements. The work is motivated by sharing sensitive data, while its stated findings establish correlation preservation and downstream usefulness.
neurips-2022-generating-multivariate-tim.tldr: COSCI-GAN coordinates time-series generation through shared latent inputs and a central discriminator to preserve relationships among channels.

paragraphs: Automatically generating training environments can help reinforcement learning agents handle a wide range of conditions. However, changing the training distribution can also change which policy appears best. In partially observed or stochastic settings, optimal behavior may depend on the deployment distribution of parameters governing inherent environmental uncertainty, making curriculum design consequential for the learning objective.

The authors formalize this problem as curriculum-induced covariate shift. They explain how shifting those uncertainty-related parameters can produce policies that are suboptimal for deployment. Sampling them directly from the intended distribution avoids that issue, but prevents the curriculum from freely adjusting their distribution to shape training.

SAMPLR addresses this tension within unsupervised environment design using a minimax regret approach. It optimizes utility under the ground-truth distribution even when curriculum choices bias the training data. The authors prove and validate in challenging domains that their approach preserves optimality for that distribution while encouraging robustness across environment settings. The result links curriculum flexibility to an explicitly grounded deployment objective.
neurips-2022-grounding-aleatoric-uncerta.tldr: SAMPLR addresses curriculum-induced distribution shift while preserving optimality under the intended deployment distribution and promoting robustness.

paragraphs: Model hubs contain pretrained networks with different architectures, training data, and learning methods. Hub-Pathway aims to draw on this variety for a target task. Applying single-model transfer methods separately to every available network can be computationally costly and fails to make full use of the hub's combined knowledge.

The framework generates pathway weights that depend on the input. These weights determine which pretrained models process a particular example and how their outputs are combined into a prediction. Training uses the target task's loss end to end, so model selection and aggregation can adapt to the requirements of individual examples.

A noisy pathway generator and an exploration loss encourage trying different routes through the hub. Each pretrained model is also further trained on the examples that activate it, allowing its knowledge to adapt to those inputs. Experiments in computer vision and reinforcement learning report state-of-the-art model-hub transfer performance. The approach makes transfer a learned coordination problem across available models.
neurips-2022-hub-pathway-transfer-learni.tldr: Hub-Pathway learns input-dependent routes and output combinations across a hub of pretrained models for transfer learning.

paragraphs: Calling a neural network invariant can mean different things depending on what is measured. Broadly, invariance concerns remaining unchanged under a transformation, while equivariance concerns changing in a corresponding way. This paper examines how those ideas apply formally to deep learning models, aiming to make claims about their behavior more precise.

The authors introduce a family of metrics for invariance and equivariance that separates these properties from loss and accuracy. This matters because a model's success on a prediction task does not, by itself, specify how its behavior relates to transformations. Dedicated measurements allow the transformation-related properties to be examined in their own right.

The metrics are used to study data augmentation and equivariant layers, two common ways of encouraging these behaviors. The investigation also considers whether pretrained initialization affects a trained model's invariance and how learned invariance extends to out-of-distribution data. The contribution provides a measurement framework and an empirical analysis of these questions; the abstract does not specify the direction of each individual conclusion.
neurips-2022-in-what-ways-are-deep-neura.tldr: The paper introduces metrics that measure neural-network invariance and equivariance separately from predictive loss and accuracy.

paragraphs: A goodness-of-fit test asks whether observed data agree with a proposed probability model. For tests based on Kernel Stein Discrepancy, the choice of kernel can affect the ability to detect disagreement. KSDAgg combines tests using multiple kernels, avoiding the loss of testing power associated with setting aside data to select one kernel.

The authors prove that the aggregated test attains the collection's smallest uniform separation rate up to a logarithmic factor. This rate describes how small a discrepancy the test can reliably detect. Under compact support and a bounded model score function, they also obtain a rate over restricted Sobolev classes matching the unrestricted minimax rate up to an iterated logarithmic factor.

The procedure uses either parametric or wild bootstrap calculations to estimate thresholds and level corrections. For bandwidth selection, it replaces arbitrary rules with aggregation over choices. Experiments on synthetic and real data report stronger performance than other leading adaptive, quadratic-time KSD tests, supporting the practical value of this theoretically motivated combination.
neurips-2022-ksd-aggregated-goodness-of-.tldr: KSDAgg combines kernel-based goodness-of-fit tests to adapt kernel choice without splitting data, with theoretical power guarantees.

paragraphs: Deep learning can require optimizing several objectives that conflict with one another. In that setting, the aim is often a diverse set of representative compromises. Reference-vector methods guide optimization toward different trade-offs, but their usefulness depends on how those directions relate to the problem's Pareto front, the set of solutions where improving one objective requires sacrificing another.

This paper identifies a mismatch between preset reference vectors and the underlying front as a source of undesirable solutions. It proposes adapting the vectors during gradient-based multi-objective optimization. The adaptation is formulated as a bilevel problem, linking the choice of guiding vectors with the optimization they influence, and is handled using an efficient solver.

The authors provide a theoretical convergence analysis and evaluate the method across an extensive range of learning scenarios. They report better performance than leading alternatives in those experiments. The approach matters because it treats the directions used to seek diverse compromises as quantities to learn, rather than assuming that an initial set already suits the problem.
neurips-2022-multi-objective-deep-learni.tldr: The method adapts reference vectors during multi-objective learning to seek more representative trade-offs between conflicting objectives.

paragraphs: Object-centric learning seeks separate entity representations from perceptual inputs. Several possible explanations can initially be equally plausible, so models often refine their representations repeatedly to distinguish among them. Training through all of those refinement steps can make optimization difficult, because the backward computation becomes tied to the entire sequence of updates.

This paper treats the refined representations as fixed points and uses the implicit function theorem to differentiate them. The resulting approach separates the forward refinement process from the backward gradient calculation. That separation allows techniques developed for implicit layers to improve the stability and tractability of learning object representations.

The authors apply the approach to the slot attention module in SLATE, a leading entity-representation method. They report improved training stability and optimization, with backpropagation taking constant space and time relative to the refinement process, and requiring only one additional line of code. The complexity claim concerns backpropagation; the central contribution is changing how refinement-based models receive their training gradients.
neurips-2022-object-representations-as-f.tldr: Implicit differentiation improves training of iterative object representations by separating refinement from backpropagation through every refinement step.

paragraphs: Filling in missing attributes in a human network can change how groups appear in the data. Marginalized groups may have more missing features, and network structure together with biases in observed features can cause imputation to exaggerate differences between groups. The paper calls this artificial increase in distinctness discrimination risk.

The authors prove that higher discrimination risk can amplify unfairness in a model trained or applied on the completed data. They formalize mean aggregation imputation as a general framework and study, theoretically and empirically, which graph conditions can make its inferred features carry high discrimination risk. This connects a data preparation operation to possible downstream fairness consequences.

They then propose a simple algorithm that guarantees low discrimination risk for mean-aggregation-imputed features while minimally sacrificing reconstruction error under the imputation objective. Evaluation considers fairness and accuracy on synthetic and real credit networks. The contribution makes group distortion an explicit target during imputation, alongside the usual objective of reconstructing missing feature values.
neurips-2022-on-the-discrimination-risk-.tldr: The paper analyzes how graph feature imputation can exaggerate group differences and proposes an algorithm with provably low discrimination risk.

paragraphs: A ReLU network with one input and one hidden layer represents a piecewise-linear function. Its effective complexity depends on how many linear regions the learned function uses. This paper studies whether gradient flow, a continuous-time form of gradient-based training, favors a relatively simple function in a binary classification problem.

The result assumes that labels come from the sign of a target network containing r neurons. With high probability over both initialization and dataset sampling, gradient flow converges in a suitably defined direction to a network with perfect training accuracy and at most O(r) linear regions. That bound on the learned function's regions also yields a generalization bound.

Under an additional assumption on the data distribution, the result holds with only mild overparameterization: network width scales roughly with r, up to logarithmic factors, independently of sample size. The finding links successful fitting and controlled function complexity in this specific setting. Its guarantee concerns directional convergence under the stated labeling and distribution conditions.
neurips-2022-on-the-effective-number-of-.tldr: Under stated assumptions, gradient flow learns a perfectly fitting univariate ReLU classifier with only O(r) linear regions.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input falls outside the kinds of data a model is intended to handle. Comparing detection methods is difficult when studies use inconsistent settings and evaluation procedures. OpenOOD addresses that evaluation problem with a unified codebase and a comprehensive benchmark organized around a generalized definition of out-of-distribution detection.

The benchmark brings together more than 30 methods from this field and related areas, including anomaly detection, open set recognition, and model uncertainty. These connections matter because techniques developed under one problem label can also apply to another. A shared framework makes those overlaps part of the comparison, rather than leaving methods separated by research terminology.

The authors' comparison indicates substantial progress in the field over the preceding years. They highlight strong potential in both preprocessing approaches and the separate, complementary category of post-hoc methods. The contribution is an evaluation resource as well as an empirical assessment: it provides a more consistent basis for judging progress and comparing approaches across neighboring detection problems.
neurips-2022-openood-benchmarking-genera.tldr: OpenOOD unifies more than 30 detection methods in a shared benchmark to make out-of-distribution evaluation more consistent and comprehensive.

paragraphs: A weak learner produces a predictor that performs slightly better than chance. The classic weak-to-strong learning problem asks how to turn that modest ability into arbitrarily high accuracy when enough training data are available. AdaBoost provides one solution, but the amount of data required remains an important measure of how efficiently such a transformation works.

This paper introduces a new conversion algorithm that reaches the same generalization bounds with less training data than AdaBoost and previous weak-to-strong learners. Generalization bounds concern performance beyond the training examples, so the improvement addresses data requirements for learning rather than merely fitting the observed sample.

The authors also establish a lower bound on sample complexity, showing that their algorithm uses the minimum possible amount of training data for the problem studied. The matching algorithm and lower bound settle this classical sample-complexity question. The optimality claim is specifically about training-data requirements for constructing a strong learner from a weak one, which is the resource the paper analyzes.
neurips-2022-optimal-weak-to-strong-lear.tldr: A new weak-to-strong learning algorithm achieves optimal training-data requirements, established by a matching sample-complexity lower bound.

paragraphs: Three common fairness criteria—demographic parity, equalized odds, and predictive rate parity—generally cannot all be satisfied exactly, except in special cases. This incompatibility often leads researchers to optimize only one or two criteria. The paper instead asks how closely a prediction system can satisfy all three when small violations are allowed.

The authors formulate post-processing as an integer-programming problem. Their framework can produce a certifiably optimal solution for simultaneously addressing multiple fairness criteria within that formulation. Allowing small departures from exact fairness creates room to search for joint improvements without contradicting the impossibility result about exact simultaneous satisfaction.

Experiments show that the post-processor can improve multiple fairness definitions at once while reducing model performance only minimally. The authors also discuss using the framework to compare models and explain their fairness properties. The contribution turns a general incompatibility into an optimization problem about achievable compromises, with certificates of optimality available for the proposed formulation.
neurips-2022-pushing-the-limits-of-fairn.tldr: An integer-programming framework seeks certifiably optimal compromises among fairness criteria by allowing small violations of exact fairness.

paragraphs: Pruning removes parts of a neural network to increase sparsity, often at some cost to accuracy. That cost need not be shared equally across classes. This paper examines changes in class recall, the share of examples from a class that are recognized correctly, and asks how pruning alters existing differences in recognition performance.

The authors hypothesize an intensification effect: classes whose recall is below overall accuracy become relatively worse after pruning, while those above accuracy become relatively better. They propose Undecayed Pruning to reduce this effect. The hypothesis centers on a class's starting performance relative to overall accuracy, extending the investigation beyond class underrepresentation alone.

Statistical analysis finds less severe intensification with the proposed algorithm. It also finds stronger intensification for more difficult tasks, less complex models, and higher pruning ratios. At lower pruning ratios, the authors observe the opposite pattern, a reduction in the disparity. These findings make the relationship conditional on the pruning setting and show why aggregate accuracy alone cannot describe the changes studied.
neurips-2022-recall-distortion-in-neural.tldr: The paper studies how pruning changes relative class recall and proposes Undecayed Pruning to attenuate observed disparity intensification.

paragraphs: A classical Markov decision process models uncertain outcomes using a known transition rule. A robust version also allows uncertainty about that rule itself. It chooses actions while considering the most adverse transition rule within a specified set, making ambiguity about system dynamics part of the decision problem.

This paper develops a solution framework for robust problems with s-rectangular ambiguity sets, a particular structure for organizing transition uncertainty by state. The framework breaks the computation into repeated robust Bellman updates and projections onto a simplex, the space of probability vectors. For ambiguity sets defined through phi-divergences, the authors exploit additional structure in those projection problems.

They show that the resulting problems can be solved substantially faster than with leading commercial solvers and a recent first-order method. The practical significance is computational: accounting for ambiguity becomes more attractive when its repeated optimization steps can be handled efficiently. The reported advantage applies to the structured robust MDP class studied, connecting a specific uncertainty model with a specialized solution procedure.
neurips-2022-robust-phi-divergence-mdps-.tldr: A structured solver accelerates robust MDPs with s-rectangular phi-divergence ambiguity sets through Bellman updates and simplex projections.

paragraphs: Dynamic link prediction concerns connections in graphs that evolve over time. This paper examines whether existing evaluations adequately test that ability. The authors introduce two visualization techniques for inspecting recurring edges and find that many connections appear again at later times, making historical repetition an important feature of the evaluation setting.

Motivated by that observation, they propose EdgeBank, a baseline based purely on memorizing edges. Its surprisingly strong performance across several settings reveals that the negative edges used in current evaluations are easy to distinguish. A method can therefore perform well in those settings using remembered connectivity, which changes how more elaborate methods' apparent strengths should be assessed.

The authors introduce two negative-sampling strategies to create more challenging comparisons and better reflect real applications. They also add six dynamic graph datasets from domains absent in existing benchmarks. Together, the visualizations, baseline, sampling procedures, and datasets provide tools for evaluating which aspects of temporal connectivity a method handles successfully.
neurips-2022-towards-better-evaluation-f.tldr: A strong memorization baseline exposes easy dynamic-link evaluations, motivating harder negative sampling and six additional datasets.

paragraphs: Person-to-person virtual try-on transfers clothing between images of people. Large changes in pose or viewpoint make that transfer difficult because the garment must be aligned across substantially different body configurations. This paper addresses weaknesses in warping methods that rely mainly on two-dimensional cues and restrict correspondence estimation to local regions.

The proposed system learns global pixel correspondences that combine semantic relationships, local deformation, and three-dimensional body geometry. Two encoders extract pose-aware and high-level representations from the source and target images. A coarse-to-fine decoder repeatedly refines the correspondences, with inferred parametric 3D human models serving as geometric priors during refinement.

An adversarial generator then receives the warped garment and target-person image to synthesize the try-on result. Experiments on public benchmarks and a selected HardPose test set report better performance than leading try-on methods. The approach connects global matching with body geometry so that garment alignment can better accommodate the challenging pose and viewpoint variations targeted by the work.
neurips-2022-towards-hard-pose-virtual-t.tldr: The method combines global image correspondences with inferred 3D body geometry to improve virtual try-on across difficult poses and viewpoints.

paragraphs: Some learning problems naturally involve inputs beyond fixed-length vectors, including functional data analysis and graph classification. This paper extends mean-field analysis of two-layer neural networks to an infinite-dimensional parameter space. The setting matters because it supports feature learning while moving beyond theories developed mainly for neurons with finitely many parameters.

The authors first derive a generalization error bound for a regularized empirical risk minimizer. With sufficiently much data, that minimizer generalizes despite the infinite-dimensional neurons. They then extend a particle optimization framework to construct two gradient-based algorithms for training these networks, linking the statistical question of generalization with the computational question of finding a solution.

Both algorithms are shown to converge to a regularized global optimum. Their convergence rates are polynomial in the online setting and exponential in the finite-sample setting, respectively. The authors identify this as, to their knowledge, the first quantitative global optimization guarantee combining infinite-dimensional inputs with feature learning. The guarantees concern the specified mean-field, regularized framework.
neurips-2022-two-layer-neural-network-on.tldr: The paper proves generalization and quantitative global optimization guarantees for regularized, two-layer mean-field networks with infinite-dimensional parameters.

paragraphs: Vision-language applications can benefit from different ways of processing images and text. A dual encoder represents them separately for efficient retrieval, while a fusion encoder supports joint processing for classification. VLMo learns both capabilities within a unified pretrained model, allowing one modular architecture to serve these different uses.

Its Multiway Transformer places modality-specific experts alongside a shared self-attention layer in every block. This arrangement combines specialized processing with a common attention mechanism. After pretraining, the model can be fine-tuned as a fusion encoder for vision-language classification or used as a dual encoder for matching images and text efficiently.

The authors also introduce staged pretraining that uses large image-only and text-only datasets in addition to paired image-text examples. This broadens the kinds of training data the unified model can exploit. Experiments report state-of-the-art results on visual question answering, NLVR2, and image-text retrieval. The results support both the architecture's flexibility across tasks and the usefulness of the proposed pretraining strategy.
neurips-2022-vlmo-unified-vision-languag.tldr: VLMo unifies dual-encoder retrieval and fusion-based vision-language processing through modality experts, shared attention, and staged pretraining.
